newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's police and rebels resume musical battle.
newsitem.headline: Peru's police and rebels resume musical battle.

text.p: Peruvian police and Marxist hostage-takers resumed their psychological warfare on the 52nd day of the crisis on Friday, blasting music at each other from either side of the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
The roughly 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, holding 72 captives, began the day with a broadcast of their revolutionary hymn in honour of dead comrades.
Then MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini bellowed through a megaphone: "On the 52nd day of the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence, what is our objective?"
"To vanquish or to die!" replied his fellow MRTA members. "Long live the MRTA!"

Later in the morning, police blared a half-hour sequence of traditional "criolla" music -- guitar-based rhythms full of patriotic slogans and eulogies to Peru -- from huge speakers directed at the residence.

In tactics reminiscent of the U.S. siege against former Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega after the 1989 invasion, Peruvian police have also on previous occasions tried to weaken the rebels' resolve by blasting them with military marches and the sound of sirens and aircraft.
The "criolla" music continued in the afternoon, with songs like "With You, Peru" and "I am in love with my Peru." Police also sent a helicopter flying over the residence twice.

The renewed musical battle -- which annoyed residents in the normally quiet, middle-class San Isidro neighbourhood -- came despite growing expectations of a resumption of face-to-face talks between the MRTA and the government.
Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani told reporters efforts to jump-start talks had "advanced positively" after he and two other mediators met on Thursday with Cerpa inside the residence.
The panel of "guarantors" also met with government negotiator Domingo Palermo later on Thursday to try to set a timetable for renewed negotiations.
The government and the MRTA have not met since their first face-to-face contact on Dec. 28.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, whose country has two dozen hostages inside the residence, said talks may be close. "I have a feeling that (preliminary talks) may get going next week," Hashimoto told ruling party leaders in Tokyo.
President Alberto Fujimori promised Hashimoto at last weekend's summit in Canada that he would resume direct talks with the rebels.
Local media also expressed a new mood of optimism. "After 52 days of anguish, light is seen at the end of the tunnel," said the daily Expreso in a front-page banner headline on Friday.

Both the government and the MRTA have stated a desire for dialogue, but the rebels are not prepared to hold direct talks unless Fujimori drops his refusal to consider their main demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
It was impossible to know the details of Thursday's meetings with the mediators as all parties have apparently agreed a policy of keeping any contact private.

Fujimori was due to leave for Britain late on Friday, where he is expected to participate in an economic conference on Monday. Government sources said Fujimori may travel to Romania afterwards, sparking speculation the East European country may figure in an asylum deal for the MRTA.

Since Fujimori floated the possibility of granting the rebels exile in exchange for laying down their arms and leaving the country, speculation has raged in local political and diplomatic circles over which country may be involved.

The heavily-armed MRTA fighters burst in on a party on Dec. 17, seizing the ambassador's mansion and hundreds of guests, including diplomats, government officials and Japanese and Peruvian businessmen.

The MRTA has since set free most of the hostages. But it has retained its most prized captives, including two government ministers, Japan's and Bolivia's ambassadors, Japanese diplomats and businessmen, and Fujimori's brother Pedro.

Two Peruvian doctors entered the residence Friday along with Red Cross officials to attend to the health problems suffered by many of the captives. "We are doing our best to provide adequate medical attention," said Red Cross spokeswoman Cecile Baux, without giving more details.
